newsitem.title: USA: Coffee hits 17-month highs, soybeans and oil fall.
newsitem.headline: Coffee hits 17-month highs, soybeans and oil fall.

text.p: Coffee prices rallied Thursday on expectations that physical supplies will remain tight due to a smaller crop in leading producer Brazil.
Oil prices fell amid warmer weather in the Northeast, the world's largest heating oil market. Grain prices fell, while lumber rose.
The Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures closed 1.24 points lower at 238.07.
Coffee prices rose amid concerns about a significantly smaller coffee crop in Brazil and possible delays in Colombia after a dockworkers strike.

"The outlook is for tighter supply because there is the potential for Brazil's crop to be sizably lower and the presumption of residual delays in Colombia after the dockworkers' strike," said Refco Inc. analyst Ann Prendergast.
At New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, March coffee futures closed up 6.25 cents a pound at 150.80 cents after setting a new life-of-contract high at 151.50 cents.
Prices are at the highest level since September 1995.
Shipments from Colombia, the No. 2 coffee exporter, were stalled last month by a two-week strike by workers at the country's top coffee port, Buenaventura.
Supply jitters there were heightened by news of a debt strike declared on Wednesday by Colombia's independent coffee growers to protest lack of debt relief from the government.
Traders were also concerned that this year's Brazilian coffee crop might fall below 20 million bags from above 26 million last year.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices dropped sharply based on views that heating oil supplies are more than ample amid declining demand and unseasonably mild weather.
"You are seeing prices taking their cue from a declining heating oil market, which is in turn a function of weather being warmer than normal," said Mike Rothman, analyst with Merrill Lynch.
March heating oil ended 1.87 cents lower at 61.45 cents a gallon, with March gasoline closing down 2.24 cents at 65.30 cents a gallon, and March crude oil down 81 cents at $23.10 a barrel.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans led grain markets lower after details of President Clinton's new budget were published and revealed projections for big crops this summer.
March soybeans closed 9-1/2 cents a bushel lower at $7.30, March corn 3-3/4 cents lower at $2.68-3/4, and March wheat 3-1/2 cents lower at $3.58.

The fiscal 1998 budget proposed for the Agriculture Department assumes plantings of 64 million acres of soybeans with production estimated at 2.42 billion bushels. Last year's output was 2.382 billion bushels.
The budget also assumes U.S. corn production will total 9.625 billion bushels. The U.S. Feed Grains Council this week had estimated production at only 9.49 billion bushels.
"Wheat and corn just followed suit," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter, referring to the collapse in soybeans.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, March lumber closed up the $10 per thousand board feet daily limit at $403.50 as the market focused on a possible pick-up in cash market demand.

Curt Cunningham, president of Pacific Futures Trading, said he had not detected a strong improvement in cash markets but with spring around the corner prices had the potential to spike upward since many lumber dealers have low stocks.
"All the business will try to be run through the keyhole at once," Cunningham said.
